lecture_context.lecture_title: What’s Going On Inside My Model?

unit.name: Frontier-model diagnostic case study and four evidence lenses
unit.description: Introduces the lecture goal and uses a failing 200B-parameter checkpoint scenario to organize evidence for understanding large-model behavior before retraining or editing code.
unit.summary: The lecture frames model understanding as a spectrum from older CNN interpretability tools to open research questions for frontier models [ts=14s]. In the checkpoint case study, the instructor asks what evidence to inspect when reasoning benchmarks regress, safety evals fail, and tool-use latency spikes [ts=157s]. Student answers are organized around error analysis, training/validation loss curves, recent training data, checkpoint comparisons, hardware/latency signals, attention maps, embeddings, sensitivity analysis, scaling laws, and MoE routing [ts=231s] [ts=629s]. The instructor consolidates the answers into four buckets: training and scaling, representations and internals, data and distribution, and capabilities and safety [ts=769s].

key_points.text: A failing frontier checkpoint should be investigated with error analysis on reasoning and safety failures before changing code or retraining.
Training loss should converge smoothly, and validation loss should follow a similar but usually slightly higher curve.
A recent batch or round of data can introduce poison, bias, or distribution changes that explain new failures.
Attention maps can be inspected in language models as relationships between tokens, but they may reveal unintuitive or suspicious token dependencies.
Scaling-law style sensitivity analysis compares compute, data, and model size to decide whether a model is undertrained, too small, or otherwise mismatched.
Mixture-of-experts models can fail if routing repeatedly selects the same expert, reducing effective capacity.

kp_catalog.name: Frontier-model diagnostic evidence lenses
kp_catalog.description: A framework for diagnosing a large-model regression using training/scaling, representations/internals, data/distribution, and capabilities/safety evidence before touching code or restarting training.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: The lecture uses the 200B checkpoint case to motivate the entire frontier-model half and organizes the answers into four diagnostic buckets [ts=157s] [ts=769s].

kp_catalog.name: Loss curves and training telemetry
kp_catalog.description: Using training loss, validation loss, gradient norms, learning-rate schedules, checkpoint trends, and hardware metrics to assess whether model training is stable.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: The instructor returns to loss curves both in the opening case and the training-diagnostics section as the natural first health check for a failing model [ts=302s] [ts=4715s].

kp_catalog.name: Attention-map and embedding diagnostics
kp_catalog.description: Inspecting attention relationships and embedding neighborhoods to sanity-check internal representations in language models.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: Attention maps are suggested in the opening case, and later the lecture identifies attention plus embeddings as the two visualizable ideas behind transformer representations [ts=542s] [ts=4621s].

kp_catalog.name: Mixture-of-experts routing diagnostics
kp_catalog.description: Monitoring expert routing and load balancing to detect underused or overused experts in MoE-style models.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: MoE routing appears in the opening case as a possible capacity failure mode and later in the final dashboard summary as a metric to monitor [ts=708s] [ts=5850s].
